units.passage: Talk to your student if you suspect that something may be amiss.
units.why: 'Talk to your student if you suspect that something may be amiss' asks instructors to talk with the student before escalating; P57, instructor, when-misuse, should.

units.passage: If I suspect you used Generative AI and you did not acknowledge that use, I reserve the right to withhold a grade until I have had a conversation with you.
units.why: 'I reserve the right to withhold a grade until I have had a conversation with you' states what happens after suspected unacknowledged use: a talk with the student first, P57.
units.fit_note: Also makes non-acknowledgment the trigger and withholds the grade as a consequence (P28, P37). The instructor may withhold the grade pending a conversation, triggered by unacknowledged AI use.

units.passage: If we suspect that AI has been used inappropriately, you will receive a written or in-person notification. The assignment in question will not be graded until you follow up with your Breakout professor.
units.why: 'you will receive a written or in-person notification. The assignment ... will not be graded until you follow up with your Breakout professor' describes procedure after suspected misuse; P57.
units.fit_note: Student is notified and must follow up; grading is held. Suspected misuse leads to written or in-person notice and an ungraded assignment until the student follows up.

units.passage: Exploratory Meeting A candid information-gathering conversation between instructor and student. This meeting is informal and does not require any advance notification or other preparatory work.
units.why: Describes an 'Exploratory Meeting' as a candid conversation between instructor and student, which is talking with the student first (P57).
units.fit_note: A definition only; it does not say when the meeting must happen.

units.passage: Always follow your research with a non-accusatory conversation with your student.
units.why: Tells instructors to follow their research with a 'non-accusatory conversation' with the student: talk first (P57).

units.passage: Identify and discuss the ways faculty might use GAI in teaching support work (outside the classroom, such as preparing syllabi, designing assignments, grading, writing letters of recommendation, etc.) and administrative tasks.
units.policy: Programs identify and discuss the ways faculty might use GAI in teaching support work outside the classroom, such as preparing syllabi, designing assignments, grading, writing letters of recommendation, and in administrative tasks.
units.why: Prompts discussion of faculty AI use 'in teaching support work (outside the classroom, such as preparing syllabi, designing assignments, grading ...)', which is P59.
units.fit_note: Discussion prompt about faculty uses; no use is permitted or banned.

units.passage: Are there any areas of GAI use the department considers inappropriate?
units.why: 'Are there any areas of GAI use the department considers inappropriate?' invites units to decide which faculty uses to rule out; P59 (instructor use of AI for teaching work) is the nearest type.
units.fit_note: Discussion question; no use is banned or permitted.

units.passage: Use generative AI to enhance teaching and learning experiences while maintaining academic integrity.
units.why: Faculty: "Use generative AI to enhance teaching and learning experiences while maintaining academic integrity" says what instructors should use AI for, P59.

units.passage: Instructors may use AI tools to assist with drafting feedback and analysis, but final academic judgments (grades, degree progress decisions, and disciplinary determinations) must always be made and confirmed by a qualified human.
units.why: "Instructors may use AI tools to assist with drafting feedback and analysis" permits instructor AI use for teaching work (P59).

units.passage: Faculty may use AI in course design, instructional materials, accessibility supports, simulations, case studies, and other learning experiences where it enhances student learning.
units.why: "Faculty may use AI in course design, instructional materials, accessibility supports, simulations, case studies" permits instructor AI use for teaching work (P59).

units.passage: AI supports, but never replaces, the instructor's expertise and professional judgment.
units.why: "AI supports, but never replaces, the instructor's expertise and professional judgment" limits instructor reliance on AI (P59).

units.passage: ChatGPT (Generative Pre-Trained Transformer) is a free Artificial Intelligence (AI) system released by Open AI that can be used to create art and music, as well as a variety of language-based tasks, such as writing essays, debugging computer code, translating between languages, explaining math problems, and many others
units.why: Explains ChatGPT as 'a free Artificial Intelligence (AI) system released by Open AI' that writes, debugs code and translates, defining the tool the page covers: P61.

units.passage: University faculty members (including part-time and visiting faculty or those on sabbatical or leave)
units.policy: The policy applies to faculty, staff and other employees, graduate assistants, guests with electronic access, third parties and students.
units.why: The scope section lists faculty, staff, contractors and 'Students' as Covered Individuals, defining who the policy binds: P61 (scope), actor all.
units.fit_note: Scope statement listing who is bound.

units.passage: Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to machine-based systems that can perform tasks that would typically require human intelligence. It often involves algorithms or models capable of learning, reasoning, and making decisions. AI can be found in a wide range of applications and technologies, from voice agents that engage in natural language processing to image recognition tools and from autonomous vehicles to virtual assistants.
units.why: The definition 'machine-based systems that can perform tasks that would typically require human intelligence' defines AI and so the scope of the policy: P61.

units.passage: A general term identifying applications, services, features, and add-ins that leverage AI to create content or otherwise support or enhance the creation of content, whether as a stand-alone application or service or as functionality embedded within another tool, platform, or service.
units.why: The 'AI Tools' definition covers 'features, and add-ins that leverage AI' including 'functionality embedded within another tool', setting scope to embedded AI too: P61 chosen over P07 because it is a definition, not a rule on editors.
units.fit_note: Definition also brings embedded AI features inside the rules (cf. P07), but says nothing about editors or IDEs.

units.passage: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI or GAI) is a subset of AI techniques that learns patterns contained in input data to generate new content that emulates the structure and characteristics of the input data but is novel content, including text, computer code, synthetic data, workflows, and models of physical objects. Generative AI also can be used to create novel art, literature, or material design.
units.why: Generative AI is defined as 'a subset of AI techniques that learns patterns contained in input data to generate new content', including computer code: P61.

units.passage: refers to AI systems capable of independently planning, initiating, and executing actions to achieve specified objectives with limited or no real-time human intervention. Agentic AI systems may use tools, access external systems or data sources, invoke other AI models, make decisions, and perform multi-step workflows autonomously or semi-autonomously. Examples include autonomous research agents, AI assistants capable of taking actions on behalf of users, and systems that interact with enterprise applications or external services.
units.why: Agentic AI is defined as 'AI systems capable of independently planning, initiating, and executing actions', setting what later agent rules cover: P61.

units.passage: (i) use of artificial intelligence tools or other tools that generate artificial content in
units.why: The unauthorized-AI definition applies to 'tools that generate artificial content' broadly, extending beyond named AI tools; it defines the scope of what counts, so P61.
units.fit_note: No standalone definition; scope is set inside the misconduct definition.

units.passage: Generally, when students see that AI is prohibited, they will consider that to mean generative AI (GenAI) tools and not editing or grammar tools.
units.why: The note says that when AI is prohibited "students will consider that to mean generative AI (GenAI) tools and not editing or grammar tools", clarifying how a ban is read and the scope of AI; closest is P61. (Final codes after reconciliation: actor instructor; see resolution_why.)
units.fit_note: It reports how students read the word AI in a ban and advises that instructors clarify editing tools. Reports how students read a ban, implying routine tools fall outside it, rather than exempting them by rule.

units.passage: Various forms of AI and machine learning have long formed a part of our academic life at Wesleyan; tools such as Google Translate are already familiar to our community as challenges to specific forms of learning, like language acquisition and writing assistance.
units.why: 'Various forms of AI and machine learning have long formed a part of our academic life ... Google Translate' sets what counts as AI and notes older tools; P61 (define AI and scope), all, general, informs.
units.fit_note: Frames scope by example (Google Translate) rather than a formal definition.

units.passage: Tools that rely on Large Language Models–such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, and the most recent versions of Grammarly–can be used not only to write and generate information but also to proofread, brainstorm, summarize documents, extract information, format and analyze data, create images, generate and debug code, and so forth.
units.why: The sentence lists what LLM tools can do (proofread, brainstorm, summarize, format and analyze data, create images, generate and debug code), delimiting the uses a policy must address; P61, all, general, informs.
units.fit_note: A: Lists tools and uses rather than defining AI. B: Describes the range of AI uses to consider rather than defining AI formally.

units.passage: This policy applies to all faculty, staff, students, and affiliates of Wesleyan University who collect, use, or share university information in AI tools and platforms.
units.why: 'applies to all faculty, staff, students, and affiliates ... who collect, use, or share university information in AI tools' sets the scope; P61, all, general, informs.
units.fit_note: Defines scope by persons and information, not a definition of AI.

units.passage: Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to the ability of a computer system to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence.
units.why: Defines AI as "the ability of a computer system to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence", a definition that sets what the framework covers (P61).

units.passage: features such as the grammar and language editor in MS Word that help us with editing tasks are based on AI.
units.why: The text notes the "grammar and language editor in MS Word" is "based on AI", widening what counts as AI; it is informational scope (P61) and not an exemption (P100) because it allows nothing.
units.fit_note: Also shows routine embedded features count as AI, but does not exempt them from the rules. Also names Alexa and Siri as AI, without saying whether embedded features fall under any rule.

units.passage: This framework focuses primarily on generative artificial intelligence.
units.why: "This framework focuses primarily on generative artificial intelligence" narrows the scope to generative AI, so P61 (definition and scope).

units.passage: Generative AI refers to machine learning models that can generate new, original content like text, images, audio, video, and more.
units.why: "Generative AI refers to machine learning models that can generate new, original content" defines the term, P61.

units.passage: Generative AI is a term that encompasses a wide variety of artificial intelligence tools that can draft or substantively edit academic work for a user
units.why: The FAQ defines generative AI as tools "that can draft or substantively edit academic work for a user", which sets the policy's scope (P61).

units.passage: Any tool that generates or substantively edits content is considered generative AI. Such tools include (but aren’t limited to) Grammarly, ChatGPT, Dall-E, Microsoft CoPilot, and Google Gemini.
units.why: "Any tool that generates or substantively edits content is considered generative AI," naming Grammarly among examples, defines the tools covered (P61).

units.passage: This policy applies to all students.
units.why: "This policy applies to all students" sets the policy's scope, P61.
units.fit_note: Scope only; the policy gives no definition of AI.

units.passage: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is a technology that can create content, including text, images, audio, or video, when prompted by a user. Generative AI systems learn patterns and relationships from massive amounts of data, which enables them to generate new content that may be similar, but not identical, to the underlying training data.
units.why: Defines generative AI (quoted from the state CIO), setting what the guidance covers (P61).
units.fit_note: Definition is quoted from the state CIO guidance.

units.passage: This Policy applies to all students, faculty, and staff at WPI.
units.why: 'This Policy applies to all students, faculty, and staff at WPI' sets who the policy binds. Scope statement, P61, the nearest type.
units.fit_note: Sets who the policy binds rather than defining AI.

units.passage: “Confidential Information” means, for the purpose of this Policy, confidential WPI institutional data, confidential WPI employee data, and WPI student data that is not publicly available and should not be released publicly, including but not limited to: • Social security numbers • Financial account information • Passwords • Driver’s license numbers • Health care information protected under HIPAA • Human Resources and personnel information • Student records protected by FERPA • Gift and Donor Information
units.policy: Confidential Information means confidential WPI institutional data, confidential WPI employee data, and WPI student data that is not publicly available and should not be released publicly, including but not limited to social security numbers, financial account information, passwords, driver's license numbers, HIPAA-protected health care information, human resources and personnel information, FERPA-protected student records, and gift and donor information.
units.why: Defines 'Confidential Information' (confidential institutional and employee data, and student data not publicly available; examples include SSNs, passwords, HIPAA and FERPA records) to set what may not be entered. Scope definition, P61.
units.fit_note: Defines the protected data category the AI ban covers, not AI or AI tools.

units.passage: Generative artificial intelligence (“AI”) is defined for purposes of this Policy as any type of software, i.e. algorithm, that is capable of creating, writing, or re-writing any form of content, including but not limited to text, artwork, graphics, imagery, audio, video, and music.
units.why: The section defines generative AI as 'any type of software... capable of creating, writing, or re-writing any form of content', which sets what the policy covers, so it is a definition (P61), informs, phase general.

units.passage: Generative AI tools are distinct from search engines in that they generate content.
units.why: 'Generative AI tools are distinct from search engines in that they generate content' draws the scope boundary between generative AI and search, which is a scope definition (P61) rather than a rule.

units.passage: Submitting content created by any of the above means, either in its original or edited form, will constitute use of generative AI.
units.why: 'Submitting content created by any of the above means, either in its original or edited form, will constitute use of generative AI' fixes that edited AI output still counts as AI use; it is a scope rule (P61) and not a ban.
units.fit_note: Also states that lightly edited AI output still counts as generative AI use, which is a scoping rule about submissions more than a definition of AI.

units.passage: Using AI on an assignment means more than having it write your text. Brainstorming, outlining, summarizing a reading, translating, or fixing code with AI all count as AI use, and the assignment's level applies to all of them.
units.why: "Brainstorming, outlining, summarizing a reading, translating, or fixing code with AI all count as AI use" defines what counts as AI use (P61).

units.passage: This policy applies to all credit-bearing courses, labs, seminars, and supervised research offered by Yeshiva College, Stern College for Women, and Sy Syms School of Business, whether delivered in person, online, or in hybrid format. It also covers students from these colleges taking credit-bearing coursework anywhere at Yeshiva University. Where an instructor's stated course policy differs from this document, the instructor's policy controls. The policy applies to all instructors who design, teach, or grade these courses, and to AI use in coursework, assessment, feedback, and grading. Supervised research, theses, and research assistantships are addressed in Section 12.
units.why: The Scope section says the policy "applies to all credit-bearing courses, labs, seminars, and supervised research" at three colleges, defining coverage (P61).

units.passage: It also does not govern AI use in institutional research, admissions, human resources, or other administrative operations, which fall under separate University policies.
units.why: "does not govern AI use in institutional research, admissions, human resources, or other administrative operations" defines a scope limit (P61).

units.passage: This policy applies to AI use in general and deliberately does not distinguish between assistive and generative AI tools. Assistive tools are increasingly built on generative engines, and the line between the categories is blurry. What matters under this policy is the level of use, not the type of tool.
units.why: "deliberately does not distinguish between assistive and generative AI tools" defines coverage by level of use rather than tool type (P61).

units.passage: Software that produces or transforms text, code, images, audio, or other content in response to a prompt or input, including chatbots, writing and coding assistants, and image, audio, and video generators.
units.why: The definition of "AI tool" ("Software that produces or transforms text, code, images, audio, or other content in response to a prompt") defines AI (P61).

units.passage: Any student or faculty work produced with meaningful help from an AI tool. Meaningful help includes generating or rewriting sentences, paragraphs, or code; producing an outline, thesis, or argument; summarizing or translating substantial text; debugging or writing code; and generating analysis or interpretation of data. It does not include the minimal uses listed below.
units.why: The definition of "AI-assisted work" lists meaningful help such as "debugging or writing code", defining what triggers the rules (P61).

units.passage: Instructors may restrict a minimal use only where it is central to what an assessment measures (for example, spelling in a language course), and must say so explicitly. Disclosure A clear written statement, in the form and location specified by the instructor or assignment, identifying any AI tools used and how they were employed in producing the work.
units.why: The definition of "Disclosure" ("A clear written statement, in the form and location specified by the instructor or assignment") defines the term (P61).
units.fit_note: Defines disclosure and lets the instructor set its form and location.

units.passage: Preparatory work is work: brainstorming, outlining, and clarifying concepts are part of an assignment, and AI assistance with them counts as AI assistance with the assignment.
units.why: "Preparatory work is work: brainstorming, outlining, and clarifying concepts are part of an assignment" clarifies that preparatory use counts as AI assistance on the assignment, a definition of coverage (P61).

units.passage: This policy contains overarching guidelines that apply to all in the YU community while pursuing their YU activities. After these general requirements, this policy includes specific guidelines related to instruction and research.
units.why: "This policy contains overarching guidelines that apply to all in the YU community" sets the policy's scope and structure (P61).

units.passage: This Generative AI policy (“Policy”) governs the use of Generative AI tools by University faculty and staff (the “YU community”) in the performance of their functions for or on behalf of YU.
units.why: The Scope says the policy "governs the use of Generative AI tools by University faculty and staff", defining coverage (P61).

units.passage: “Internal or Restricted Information” means any business or technical information or research result belonging to YU, a YU faculty or staff member, collaborators or other third parties, that is not publicly known or that has been provided or received under an obligation to maintain the information as Internal or Restricted. Please note this includes Protected Health Information or PHI.
units.why: "means any business or technical information or research result belonging to YU" defines Internal or Restricted Information, which sets what may not be input, P61.

units.passage: “Generative AI” includes any machine-based tool designed to consider user questions, prompts, and other inputs (e.g., text, images, videos) to generate a human-like output (e.g., a response to a question, a written document, software code, or a product design).
units.why: "includes any machine-based tool designed to consider user questions, prompts, and other inputs" defines Generative AI for the policy, P61.

units.passage: “Personal Information” means any information that, whether alone or in combination with other available information, identifies, relates to, describes, is reasonably capable of being associated with, or could reasonably be linked, directly or indirectly, to an individual.
units.why: The definition of "Personal Information" fixes what staff may not enter into AI tools (P61).

units.passage: Ongoing discussions in the program should include peer and other professional association guidance on the appropriate use of GAI technologies in these areas, especially as might impact the evaluation of activities in line with tenure and promotion criteria.
units.policy: Ongoing discussions in the program should include peer and other professional association guidance on the appropriate use of GAI technologies in teaching, research, scholarship, creative activities and administrative tasks, especially as might impact the evaluation of activities in line with tenure and promotion criteria.
units.why: 'Ongoing discussions in the program should include peer and other professional association guidance on the appropriate use of GAI technologies', especially for tenure and promotion. It concerns faculty AI use in teaching, research and evaluation (P62, partly).
units.fit_note: Covers teaching, research and evaluation of faculty work, not only research

units.passage: What are emerging professional standards in our fields for GAI in research, publishing, citation, and intellectual and creative authorship?
units.policy: What are emerging professional standards in our fields for GAI in research, publishing, citation, and intellectual and creative authorship?
units.why: Asks about 'emerging professional standards ... for GAI in research, publishing, citation, and ... authorship', i.e. AI in research and scholarship (P62).
units.fit_note: Discussion question.

units.passage: The key difference is that, in cases where the use of AI is permitted, undergraduate students may use AI as a support tool, whereas in graduate courses, the use of AI must be approached with more caution since such usage in scholarly publications is prohibited, at least for now, and depending on the journal.
units.why: For graduate courses, AI use 'must be approached with more caution since such usage in scholarly publications is prohibited, at least for now'; this ties the rule to publication norms (P62).
units.fit_note: Concerns graduate coursework as preparation for scholarship, not research itself. Graduate coursework caution grounded in journal rules.

units.passage: In accordance with the Use of Human Subjects in Research Policy , faculty, students, and staff conducting research should ensure that they do not input into generative AI tools any information collected for specific limited purposes, such as research data or information where a person’s identity is or could easily be connected to the data.
units.why: Research rule: those conducting research 'should ensure that they do not input into generative AI tools any information collected for specific limited purposes, such as research data'; governs research, P62.

units.passage: Do NOT put confidential research data into AI tools as it may be considered a public disclosure for the purposes of intellectual property rights.
units.why: 'Do NOT put confidential research data into AI tools as it may be considered a public disclosure for the purposes of intellectual property rights' concerns research data; P62 best matches because it is about research data, though it is also a data and IP warning.
units.fit_note: Also a data-privacy and IP-disclosure warning (P50/P52). A ban on entering confidential research data because it counts as public disclosure; overlaps with P62 (research) and P50 (data).

units.passage: Many journals and publishing agencies have specific policies regarding AI use by authors and reviewers. It is your responsibility to both know and follow those policies.
units.why: 'It is your responsibility to both know and follow those policies' of journals and publishers on AI use by authors and reviewers: defers to venue rules for scholarship, P62.

units.passage: Clear statement by the IRB on how AI may be used and/or disclosed when conducting research.
units.why: "Clear statement by the IRB on how AI may be used and/or disclosed when conducting research" asks the institution to set research rules, P62.

units.passage: Faculty are open about their use of AI in support of research and manuscript development.
units.why: "Faculty are open about their use of AI in support of research and manuscript development" is a faculty research-disclosure norm, P62.

units.passage: The framework in Section 6 applies to supervised research, senior theses, independent studies, and research assistantships, with the supervisor in the instructor's role.
units.why: "The framework in Section 6 applies to supervised research, senior theses, independent studies, and research assistantships" extends the levels to research work, P62.

units.passage: The framework in Section 6 applies to supervised research, senior theses, independent studies, and research assistantships, with the supervisor in the instructor's role. The default is UG 0 unless the supervisor states otherwise in writing at the outset of the project.
units.why: "The default is UG 0 unless the supervisor states otherwise in writing" applies the framework and default to supervised research and theses (P62).
units.fit_note: Applies to supervised research and theses, with the supervisor in the instructor's role.

units.passage: Supervisors and students should discuss AI expectations early, revisit them as the project develops, and record any agreed departures from the default. Disclosure follows the norms of the relevant discipline in addition to the requirements of Section 7.
units.why: "Supervisors and students should discuss AI expectations early, revisit them... and record any agreed departures" sets research-supervision practice (P62).
units.fit_note: Also asks for revisiting and recording agreed departures from the default.

units.passage: Disclosure follows the norms of the relevant discipline in addition to the requirements of Section 7.
units.why: "Disclosure follows the norms of the relevant discipline in addition to the requirements of Section 7" sets research disclosure norms, P62.

units.passage: As with other tools and research methods, individuals who use Generative AI in research must be transparent regarding its use, in describing methods, acknowledgements, or elsewhere, as appropriate.
units.why: "individuals who use Generative AI in research must be transparent regarding its use" requires disclosure in research (P62).

units.passage: Researchers are responsible for the accuracy of any content created by AI that is included in any research output and must use caution in utilizing AI output in research.
units.why: "Researchers are responsible for the accuracy of any content created by AI that is included in any research output" sets research accountability (P62).

units.passage: Researchers are expected to follow the policies of journals, funding agencies and professional societies through which they report their research. For example, some journals, such as Science, currently explicitly prohibit text, figures, images or graphics generated by ChatGPT or any other AI tools.
units.why: "Researchers are expected to follow the policies of journals, funding agencies and professional societies" defers to venue rules (P62).

units.passage: Researchers must avoid uploading, or using as input, any unpublished research data
units.why: "Researchers must avoid uploading, or using as input, any unpublished research data" bans uploading unpublished data (P62 over P50 because it sits in the research section).

units.passage: This includes, e.g., unpublished manuscripts or funding proposals that researchers may be asked to peer review. NIH and NSF, among others, prohibit using Generative AI for peer review.
units.why: "NIH and NSF, among others, prohibit using Generative AI for peer review", with the ban on uploading manuscripts and proposals, sets a peer-review rule (P62).

units.passage: This also includes the Personal Information of research subjects. For example, inputting interview data to perform preliminary analysis creates the possibility that quotations or other information from research subjects could become public, and potentially, that subjects could also be identified.
units.why: "This also includes the Personal Information of research subjects" bars entering subject data in AI tools in research (P62).

units.passage: ITLE will be working to develop additional resources and helping support faculty and instructors regarding ChatGPT and other generative AI software.
units.policy: ITLE will be working to develop additional resources and helping support faculty and instructors regarding ChatGPT and other generative AI software.
units.why: "ITLE will be working to develop additional resources and helping support faculty" commits the center to support faculty with AI, P63.

units.passage: Contact us if you need additional support or resources relating to the use of Chat GPT and other AI software.
units.policy: Faculty can contact ITLE for additional support or resources relating to the use of ChatGPT and other AI software.
units.why: "Contact us if you need additional support or resources" offers consultation with ITLE for AI questions, P63.

units.passage: Because generative AI is a constantly evolving space, the committee encourages USC’s instructors to begin to learn more about generative AI so they can better adjust their pedagogy and evolve as educators.
units.why: 'the committee encourages USC's instructors to begin to learn more about generative AI so they can better adjust their pedagogy': P63 (support faculty in learning AI), should.

units.passage: Consult with
units.policy: Instructors consult peers and other professional resources for best practices.
units.why: 'Consult with peers and other professional resources for best practices' tells instructors to seek outside advice when writing policy. P63 (support faculty in learning AI) is nearest; P109 does not fit because it is about aligning rules, not seeking advice.
units.fit_note: Peer consultation by instructors rather than institutional workshops or support. | Coder B (P109): Consultation for best practices, not explicitly alignment of rules across sections

units.passage: The University should empower instructors to investigate and explore GAI tools and to
units.policy: The University should empower instructors to investigate and explore GAI tools and to develop pedagogical skills for equipping their students to engage thoughtfully with the use and implications of GAI through a range of ongoing professional development opportunities.
units.why: 'The University should empower instructors to investigate and explore GAI tools' through 'professional development opportunities': support for faculty learning (P63).

units.passage: The AI Working Group for Academics recommends the Provost, Deans, and other academic leaders support the generation of GAI Discussion Frameworks among faculty connected by school, department, area, or program.
units.policy: The AI Working Group for Academics recommends the Provost, Deans, and other academic leaders support the generation of GAI Discussion Frameworks among faculty connected by school, department, area, or program.
units.why: Recommends leaders 'support the generation of GAI Discussion Frameworks among faculty', i.e. faculty communities that learn about AI (P63).
units.fit_note: Faculty discussion groups at unit level; support is organisational rather than workshops or advice. | Coder B (P109): Recommends program-level faculty conversations; it does not ask instructors to align their rules

units.passage: As a reminder to our faculty and course instructors, you do not need to work in isolation on adapting your course(s) to the new AI landscape. The WSU Writing Program has guidance on writing with AI that is available here, the Transformational Change Initiative leads PIT Stops related to AI, and the Global Innovations Group also has trainings and workshops available. There are also general AI trainings available in Percipio.
units.why: The memo lists the Writing Program, PIT Stops and workshops so instructors "do not need to work in isolation"; this is faculty support for adapting to AI, P63.

units.passage: If you have questions about the academic integrity process, you can schedule an instructor consultation to have your questions answered.
units.why: The memo says instructors can "schedule an instructor consultation" about the academic integrity process, which is support for faculty (P63).
units.fit_note: Support is about the integrity process, not learning about AI.

units.passage: Faculty and staff need to make a point of trying out an AI tool or system so that they know how it works and what its capabilities are. Entering a low-stakes assignment, for example, can show faculty how the AI produces content and suggest something about its quality.
units.why: The report says faculty and staff "need to make a point of trying out an AI tool" so they know its capabilities, advice that instructors learn AI before setting policy (P63).

units.passage: The OTL has offered several workshops and outreach opportunities for faculty to engage with one another.
units.why: The report states 'The OTL has offered several workshops and outreach opportunities for faculty', a fact about faculty support (P63).

units.passage: Faculty need to learn all the aspects of the integrated AI tools prior to its use in the classroom. This should include the biases of the tools.
units.why: The report says faculty "need to learn all the aspects of the integrated AI tools prior to its use in the classroom", including bias, advice that instructors learn AI first (P63).

units.passage: Consult colleagues, explore pedagogical research in your discipline, reach out to the Office for Teaching & Learning (OTL) on best practices in creating assignments.
units.why: The advice to "consult colleagues, explore pedagogical research in your discipline, reach out to the Office for Teaching & Learning (OTL)" points instructors to support (P63).

units.passage: Faculty can work with instructional designers in the TLC to develop strategies engaging with generative AI in specific teaching contexts.
units.why: "Faculty can work with instructional designers in the TLC to develop strategies" offers faculty support, P63.

units.passage: 8. In Cases of Allegations of Academic Honesty Violations, the Standard of Proof is a Preponderance of the Evidence
units.policy: In academic honesty hearings, the AHB must conclude, based on all the evidence in the record, that it is more likely than not that the student engaged in a violation before the student is held responsible.
units.why: 'the standard of proof is a Preponderance of the Evidence' and the AHB 'must conclude' it is 'more likely than not' before holding a student responsible; it binds the Board and sets an evidence standard (P69).
units.fit_note: Applies to all academic honesty hearings, not only AI cases.

units.passage: Academic Technology & User Services (ATUS) and the Center for Instructional Innovation (CII) recommend a multiple-measures approach when evaluating student work. Educators are the closest to their instructional content and their students. Evaluation, therefore, should begin with instructors using their own best judgment about the student's writing.
units.why: A "multiple-measures approach" starting with "instructors using their own best judgment" sets how to weigh evidence of misuse, P69.
units.fit_note: Recommends combining several kinds of evidence rather than stating a standard of proof.

units.passage: In cases when unauthorized use of generative AI is suspected, the instructor must carefully review the content for signs of such use.
units.why: 'the instructor must carefully review the content for signs of such use' sets how suspected AI misuse is identified: by instructor review, not a tool. It is detection by evidence (P40 nearest), and the fit note says no tool is named.
units.fit_note: Requires careful instructor review of the content but does not say what evidence suffices; no software, commit history or logs are named.

units.passage: The decision as to whether generative AI has been used by a student will be based on the instructor’s subject matter expertise and discretion.
units.why: 'based on the instructor's subject matter expertise and discretion' sets the evidence basis for a finding of AI use as the instructor's judgment, which is an evidence standard (P69).

units.passage: The University's existing standard of proof applies.
